title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 18 (Conversion of companies already registered)

content.overview: Section 18 permits a company of any class registered under the Companies Act to convert into another class by altering its memorandum and articles in accordance with Chapter II. The Registrar closes the former registration and issues a new certificate after statutory compliance, while pre-conversion debts, liabilities, obligations and contracts continue unaffected.
content.glance: Conversion is achieved through alteration of the memorandum and articles; the Registrar closes the former registration and issues a certificate after compliance; existing obligations continue.
content.study: Section 18 provides the statutory mechanism for conversion of a company from one class to another. The company must alter its memorandum and articles in accordance with Chapter II. On application, the Registrar must be satisfied that the applicable registration provisions have been complied with, close the former registration, register the altered documents and issue a certificate of incorporation in the same manner as on first registration. Conversion does not extinguish or novate debts, liabilities, obligations or contracts incurred before conversion; they remain enforceable as if the conversion had not occurred.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 18 provides the statutory mechanism for conversion of a company from one class to another. The company must alter its memorandum and articles in accordance with Chapter II. On application, the Registrar must be satisfied that the applicable registration provisions have been complied with, close the former registration, register the altered documents and issue a certificate of incorporation in the same manner as on first registration. Conversion does not extinguish or novate debts, liabilities, obligations or contracts incurred before conversion; they remain enforceable as if the conversion had not occurred.

Key statutory components:
1. Power and method of conversion — A company of any class registered under the Act may convert into another class by altering its memorandum and articles in accordance with Chapter II.
2. Registrar's role — On application, the Registrar must satisfy himself that the applicable Chapter II registration provisions have been complied with, close the former registration, register the altered documents and issue a certificate of incorporation.
3. Continuity of liabilities and contracts — Conversion does not affect debts, liabilities, obligations or contracts incurred or entered into before conversion. They remain enforceable as if the registration had not been changed.
4. Application test — Identify the original and proposed class, required memorandum/articles alterations, applicable Chapter II compliance, Registrar application and the pre-existing obligations that survive conversion.
